passages.title: Taking a solvent mixture apart
paragraphs: In an ideal liquid mixture each component contributes vapour in proportion to how much of the liquid it is. Raoult's law states the contribution of component i as its mole fraction in the liquid multiplied by the vapour pressure of the pure liquid at that temperature, and the total pressure above the mixture is the sum of those contributions. Because the more volatile component contributes more vapour per mole present, the vapour standing above the liquid is always richer in that component than the liquid itself. Distillation is nothing more than the repeated exploitation of that difference.

A laboratory takes a plant extract up in a mixture of hexane and toluene and must recover the two solvents separately. Table 1 gives the normal boiling point of each pure solvent and its vapour pressure at 50 °C. A sample in which hexane accounts for 0.60 of the moles present is warmed to 50 °C in a closed flask and the pressure above it is measured.

When vapour is drawn off and condensed, the liquid left in the pot loses the volatile component faster than the other, so the pot grows steadily richer in toluene and the temperature needed to keep it boiling climbs. One evaporation and one condensation, which is all a simple still provides, therefore cannot deliver either solvent pure. A fractionating column packed with beads repeats the evaporation and condensation many times over its length, and each repetition applies the enrichment again to a vapour that is already enriched.

The measured total pressure above the 0.60 mixture at 50 °C is 300 torr, some 23 torr above the Raoult prediction. Raoult's law assumes that a molecule is as strongly attracted to an unlike neighbour as to a like one. Where that assumption fails, the mixture departs from the predicted pressure in the direction set by which attraction is the weaker.

passages.title: An unknown ester in a proton spectrum
paragraphs: A student esterifies a carboxylic acid with an alcohol, distils the product and finds a molecular formula of C₄H₈O₂ by mass spectrometry. Four compounds share that formula: butanoic acid, propyl formate, methyl propanoate and ethyl acetate. A proton NMR spectrum settles the question, because it reports three independent things about every set of equivalent protons in the molecule.

The chemical shift says how much electron density surrounds the proton. An electronegative atom nearby withdraws that density and leaves the proton less shielded from the applied field, so its signal moves downfield to a larger shift. A methyl group attached only to carbon resonates near 0.9 ppm; a methyl next to a carbonyl carbon near 2.1 ppm; a methyl or methylene bonded to an ester oxygen near 3.7 ppm and 4.1 ppm respectively. The integration gives the number of protons in the set. The multiplicity counts the protons on neighbouring carbons: n equivalent neighbours split a signal into n + 1 lines. Protons within one equivalent set do not split each other, and coupling dies away across more than three bonds, so protons on opposite sides of the ester oxygen appear as though the other set were not there.

Table 1 records the spectrum of the product. The three integrations account for all eight protons of the formula, and no signal appears downfield of 5 ppm, which already rules out the aldehyde proton of a formate ester near 8 ppm and the acid proton of a carboxylic acid, which is usually broad and well downfield of 10 ppm.

figure.caption: Table 1  Proton NMR spectrum of the product, recorded in deuterated chloroform.

passages.title: Counting a labelled antibody by light
paragraphs: An antibody is tagged with fluorescein so that it can be both quantified and located. The dye absorbs most strongly at 494 nm, and the Beer-Lambert law relates the absorbance there to the concentration: absorbance is the molar absorptivity multiplied by the concentration and by the path length the light travels through the sample. Absorbance is defined as the logarithm of the ratio of incident to transmitted intensity, so it is a ratio of two intensities and does not depend on how bright the lamp is. Table 1 lists the molar absorptivity of the conjugate at three wavelengths.

Fluorescence follows a different route. A molecule that has absorbed a 494 nm photon reaches an excited electronic state carrying vibrational energy as well. That vibrational energy is given up to the solvent within picoseconds, long before the molecule emits, so the photon that leaves is of lower energy than the one absorbed and the emission maximum sits at 519 nm. The fraction of absorbed photons that are re-emitted, the quantum yield, is 0.92 for fluorescein in alkaline buffer. Emission is collected at right angles to the exciting beam and against a nominally dark field, whereas absorbance must be read as a small difference between two large intensities.

A stock of the conjugate is diluted 50-fold and read in a cuvette of 1.00 cm path length. The absorbance at 494 nm is 0.44. The group then asks whether the same instrument could detect the conjugate at 1 nM, the concentration expected in the binding experiment they plan next.

passages.title: The jaw as a lever
paragraphs: The mandible turns about the temporomandibular joint, and the masseter is the muscle that closes it. The muscle inserts on the jaw 4.0 cm from the joint and pulls very nearly at right angles to the bone. A tooth meets food somewhere further along the same bone, so the jaw is a lever with its fulcrum at the joint, its effort applied by the muscle at 4.0 cm and its load supplied by the food. Holding the jaw still against the food means the two torques about the joint are equal: the muscle force multiplied by 4.0 cm equals the bite force multiplied by the distance from the joint to the tooth.

Investigators placed a force transducer between the teeth of a volunteer at three positions along the jaw and asked for a maximum bite at each. The masseter force was estimated at 700 N from the muscle's cross-sectional area. Table 1 gives the distance of each tooth from the joint and the bite force recorded there.

The arrangement puts the effort between the fulcrum and the load, and the effort arm is the shorter of the two, so the bite force is always smaller than the muscle force. What the jaw buys in exchange is movement: a small rotation at the joint sweeps the incisors through a much larger distance than it sweeps the molars, and at a correspondingly higher speed. Only the component of muscle force perpendicular to the bone generates torque, so a muscle whose line of pull tilts away from the perpendicular loses the cosine of that angle, which costs very little until the angle grows large.

passages.title: Reading pH with a glass electrode
paragraphs: A pH meter is a voltmeter. Its sensing electrode ends in a thin bulb of glass whose two faces sit in solutions of different hydrogen ion activity, and the hydration layers of the glass develop a potential difference across the membrane in response to that difference. A second electrode of fixed potential completes the cell. The Nernst equation gives the cell potential as a constant minus the product of a slope and the pH of the sample, and the slope is 2.303RT/F, which comes to 59.2 mV per pH unit at 25 °C. The slope is proportional to absolute temperature, so at 37 °C it is 61.5 mV per pH unit.

The constant in that expression is not a constant for long. It gathers the potential of the reference electrode, the junction potential where the reference meets the sample, and an asymmetry potential that drifts as the glass ages and that changes whenever the bulb is cleaned. The instrument is therefore calibrated against standard buffers immediately before use. Table 1 gives the potentials a freshly calibrated assembly produced in three standards and in a sample, all at 25 °C.

Two further limits matter in practice. The electrode responds to hydrogen ion activity rather than to concentration, so a sample of high ionic strength reads a higher pH than its formal concentration would suggest. And because the slope depends on temperature while the asymmetry potential does not, every assembly has an isopotential point, a pH at which the reading does not shift when the temperature changes. For the assembly in Table 1 that point lies at pH 7.00. A sample measured at a temperature other than the calibration temperature is misread by an amount that grows with its distance from that pH.

figure.caption: Table 1  Potentials recorded at 25 °C with a freshly calibrated electrode.

passages.title: Two nucleophiles and one carbonyl
paragraphs: A carbonyl group is polarised: oxygen holds the shared electrons more tightly and leaves the carbon electron-poor and open to attack. A nucleophile adds to that carbon, the double bond collapses onto the oxygen, and the result is a tetrahedral alkoxide that picks up a proton on workup. Which nucleophile adds decides what the product is. Borohydride and aluminium hydride deliver a hydride ion, which brings no carbon with it and so converts an aldehyde to a primary alcohol and a ketone to a secondary one. A Grignard reagent delivers a carbanion-like carbon, which forms a new carbon-carbon bond and lifts the substitution of the product by one.

The two hydride reagents are not interchangeable. NaBH₄ is mild enough to be used in methanol and reduces aldehydes and ketones while leaving esters and amides alone. An ester carbonyl is the poorer electrophile because the lone pair of its alkoxy oxygen is delocalised into the carbonyl, and the aluminium-hydrogen bond of LiAlH₄ is the more willing hydride donor, so esters fall to LiAlH₄ but not to NaBH₄. Table 1 sets out what each reagent does to a ketone and to an ester.

A Grignard reagent brings a second requirement. Its carbon is not only nucleophilic but strongly basic, so any oxygen-hydrogen or nitrogen-hydrogen bond in the flask protonates it and destroys it, releasing the hydrocarbon. The reagent is made and used in rigorously dry ether, and a substrate carrying a free hydroxyl or a carboxylic acid consumes a full equivalent before any addition can occur.

In the experiment that follows, 2-butanone is treated in one flask with NaBH₄ in methanol and in another with CH₃MgBr in dry ether followed by dilute aqueous acid. The carbonyl carbon of the ketone is trigonal and planar, so a nucleophile may arrive at either of its two faces with equal ease.

passages.title: What sets the finest detail a microscope can show
paragraphs: No lens images a point as a point. Light leaving a point object reaches the lens as a spreading wave, the lens collects only the part of it that falls within a cone, and what forms in the image plane is a bright disc ringed by fainter circles. Two point objects whose discs overlap substantially are recorded as one. Abbe's limit puts the smallest resolvable separation at the wavelength divided by twice the numerical aperture of the objective, where the numerical aperture is the refractive index of the medium between specimen and lens multiplied by the sine of the half-angle of the cone the lens collects.

Both terms in that expression are worth attention. A dry objective works through air, so its numerical aperture cannot exceed one and in practice stops near 0.95. Immersion oil of refractive index 1.52 fills the gap instead, and an objective designed for it reaches 1.40. Table 1 lists four objectives with the limit each reaches in green light of 550 nm. Shorter wavelengths resolve finer detail in proportion, which is why ultraviolet microscopy was pursued and why an electron beam, whose de Broglie wavelength is thousands of times shorter still, resolves atoms.

What magnification does is spread the image over more of the detector. Beyond the point where the diffraction-limited detail is comfortably sampled, further magnification enlarges the discs along with everything else and adds nothing; microscopists call it empty magnification. The information about the finest spacings in a specimen is carried by light diffracted through the largest angles, and only a lens whose cone is wide enough to gather that light can reconstruct them.

To test an oil objective of numerical aperture 1.40, a technician images fluorescent beads scattered on a coverslip and measures the separations she can and cannot resolve in green light. Two beads 150 nm apart are recorded as a single spot.

passages.title: Measuring what a kidney clears
paragraphs: The clearance of a solute is the volume of plasma that would have to be stripped completely of that solute each minute to account for the amount appearing in the urine. It is calculated as the urine concentration multiplied by the urine flow and divided by the plasma concentration, and it has the units of a flow. A solute that is filtered freely at the glomerulus and then neither reabsorbed from the tubule nor secreted into it has a clearance equal to the glomerular filtration rate, and inulin is the standard for that reason.

Filtration itself is bulk flow through a porous barrier, driven by the balance of pressures across it. Blood in the glomerular capillary pushes outward at about 55 mmHg. Fluid already in Bowman's space pushes back at about 15 mmHg, and the plasma proteins, which are too large to cross, hold water back osmotically with a colloid osmotic pressure of about 28 mmHg. The filtration rate is the product of the net pressure that remains and a filtration coefficient set by the area and permeability of the barrier.
A patient's urine was collected at a steady 1.2 mL/min while plasma and urine were sampled for five solutes. Table 1 gives the concentrations and, for four of them, the clearance that follows.

The pattern of clearances reads as a summary of what the tubule does. A clearance below the filtration rate means that part of what was filtered came back; glucose, which is reabsorbed completely until its transporters saturate, is cleared at zero. A clearance above the filtration rate means that the tubule added solute to the filtrate by secretion. Para-aminohippurate is both filtered and secreted so efficiently that nearly all of it is removed in one pass, and its clearance approximates the plasma flow through the kidney rather than the filtration rate.

figure.caption: Table 1  Plasma and urine concentrations at a urine flow of 1.2 mL/min.

passages.title: The barrier an enzyme lowers
paragraphs: Transition state theory describes a reaction as a journey over a barrier. Reactants that collide with the right geometry pass through a single arrangement of highest energy, the transition state, in which the bonds being broken are part broken and the bonds being made are part made. That arrangement sits at a maximum of the energy profile, so it cannot be isolated or trapped; it is not an intermediate, which would sit in a minimum of its own. The fraction of collisions carrying enough energy to reach the transition state falls off exponentially with the height of the barrier and rises with temperature, which is why the rate constant depends on the barrier through an exponential term in Eₐ/RT.

Figure 1 shows the profile for a reaction run with and without its enzyme. Uncatalysed, the forward barrier is 80 kJ/mol. The enzyme lowers it to 50 kJ/mol. The reactant and product levels are the same in both profiles, and the reaction releases 30 kJ/mol overall. Because a catalyst alters the barrier and not the levels on either side of it, the forward and reverse barriers fall by exactly the same amount, the forward and reverse rates rise by the same factor, and the equilibrium constant is left as it was.

How an enzyme achieves the reduction is a question about binding. An enzyme that bound its substrate very tightly and the transition state no better would hold the substrate in a deeper well and so raise the barrier out of it. What accelerates the reaction is binding that is tighter to the transition state than to the substrate, since that lowers the top of the barrier relative to the bottom. The prediction follows at once: a stable molecule shaped to imitate the transition state should bind far more tightly than one shaped like the substrate, and such transition-state analogues are among the most potent enzyme inhibitors known.

passages.title: Adding up a metabolic route
paragraphs: Enthalpy is a state function, so the enthalpy change between a given set of reactants and a given set of products is the same whatever route connects them. Hess's law is that statement put to work: a reaction nobody can run cleanly in a calorimeter can still be measured, provided its reactants and products can each be burned. Burning every compound in the equation converts them all to the same final products, carbon dioxide and water, so the enthalpy of the reaction of interest is the sum of the combustion enthalpies of its reactants minus the sum of the combustion enthalpies of its products, each weighted by its coefficient.

Table 1 lists standard combustion enthalpies for four compounds of metabolic interest. Two anaerobic routes for glucose can be assembled from them. A working muscle reduces glucose to two molecules of lactic acid; a yeast cell ferments the same glucose to two molecules of ethanol and two of carbon dioxide. Both routes leave the carbon far from fully oxidised, and both can be compared with complete oxidation of glucose, for which the combustion enthalpy in the table is itself the answer.

Two cautions belong with any such calculation. The enthalpy change is not the free energy change, and it is the free energy change that sets how much work a cell can extract and in which direction a reaction will run; the two differ by the temperature multiplied by the entropy change. And the energy a cell captures as ATP is only a fraction of the energy released, the rest appearing as heat. A Hess cycle gives the total change along a route; it says nothing about how much of that change a cell has arranged to collect.
